articles.headline: LET US SING.
articles.text:
If solid comfort you would find,
Don't forget to bear in mind,
The way to travel in or out
Is by the new Medora route.

For the coaches are the best
To recline and take your rest.
And the agents, you will find,
Are the best of human kind.

The coaches come and go on time,
Bringing in from every clime,
The honest mining sons of toil,
And the tillers of the soil.

Likewise maidens brave and fair,
Also babes with curly hair;
And Chinaman with silken queues,
And honest Cornishman and Jews.

And if you're going in or out,
Don't forget to take this route
And if your purse is flush or lank,
Call next door to Merchants bank.

We can handle by express
All the wealth that you possess,
Either packages or cash,
Gin, wine, rum or sour mash.

We will feed you at home stations
On the very best of rations;
Serve it up on nice clean plates
At the very lowest rates.

The natural beauties of this route,
You can bet, without a doubt,
Is only equaled night or day
By the vale of Yosemite.

If information you would seek
Do not fear to come and speak,
For we love to answer questions
And charge nothing for suggestions.

For dealing fair by patrons,
Be they misses maids or matrons,
We will get our share no doubt
O'er this grand Medora route.
—[Deadwood Pioneer.
articles.summary: A reprinted Deadwood Pioneer poem praising the new Medora–Deadwood stage route, its coaches, express service and home stations.

articles.text: Mr. John Kelly, the celebrated California vocalist, has arrived with his wife, and was about to pass by, as no piano or organ was to be had. He was, however, persuaded to stop and give an entertainment to-morrow night in the dining-room of Hotel de Mores, kindly tendered him by Mr. Fitzgerald. The price of admission has been reduced to 50 cents. Doors open at 7:30, performance to commence at 8 sharp.
articles.summary: California vocalist John Kelly will give an entertainment in the Hotel de Mores dining-room.

articles.text: George Grinnell, well known throughout this region, was reported to have been hanged by the Montana Stranglers recently. He is spoken of here as a man who would not steal cattle, and it seems to be a case of personal enmity. The leader of the stranglers and Grinnell had some difficulty in dividing buffalo robes a few years ago, and it is supposed that the hanging was the result of this misunderstanding.
articles.summary: George Grinnell was reported hanged by Montana stranglers, supposedly over an old quarrel about buffalo robes.

articles.text: A passenger on last Saturday's east bound train saw a herd of buffalo grazing about four miles from here. He became terrible excited, and could hardly wait for the train to reach Belfield, so anxious was he to take a shot at the buffalo. Before leaving Belfield, he telegraphed the information to several of our ambitious hunters, and they also became worked up. There was a sudden demand for horses, and the way they flew around we supposed a large herd was near here. Finally a cloud of dust was seen in the eastern part of town, but it was hard to tell whether the Marquis de Mores or William VanDriesche would get the first shot. In about an hour they returned, and seemed surprised to hear that a buffalo hunt had been organized, but it was afterwards learned that Howard Eaton's tame buffalo had a narrow escape. Howard says he will have them whitewashed and a lantern with a red light attached to them, and hopes that this will be sufficient to save the lives of his pets.
articles.summary: A rail passenger's report of buffalo near Medora set off a hunt that turned out to be Howard Eaton's tame buffalo.

articles.text: Horses are not injured by labor any more than men, and it is only by exposure, overexertion and neglect that they become jaded out at a time when they should be in their best condition for usefulness.—[Col. L. S. Record.

articles.text: Western stockmen who buy young eastern stock cattle must be prepared to shelter them the first winter from the severe storms. No greater mistake can be made than to compel unacclimated calves and ill conditioned yearlings to rustle for themselves and have no shelter from the winter storms.—[Kansas Cowboy.
articles.summary: Clipped advice to shelter eastern stock cattle their first winter.

articles.text: Advices from the vicinity of Chanpaign, Ill., say that hog cholera is raging to an alarming extent along the Sangamon river. In Sangamon township, in Piatt, county, John Madden has lost 100 head, and many others each from 40 to 100. In Goose Creek township, H. F. Dillon has lost 200 head, H. S. McFadden, 150 and others have lost heavily.

articles.text: Stallions on exhibition in Scotland are not awarded premiums as in this country. The awards are decided there by their get, which circumstance actually excludes the uncertain foal getter from successful competition. This is certainly a much more thorough test of merit than the American system, and that far at least is a decided improvement upon it.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipped note on Scottish stallion premiums.

articles.text: And now comes Benjamin F. Butler in his new role of cattle king. If Ben cannot be President of the United States he can get up the boss cattle company. We are glad to welcome Ben as a cattle man. The New York and Boston Cattle company was incorporated the other day with a capital stock of $6,000,000, and Benjamin F. Butler, of Boston, heading the directory of the company. The company will operate in Kansas, Colorado, Texas, Arozona, New Mexico and Wyoming.—[Drovers' News.
articles.summary: Clipped report that Benjamin F. Butler heads the new New York and Boston Cattle company.

articles.text: The warden of the Manitoba penitentiary, at Stony Mountain, near Winnipeg, has a fine herd of hybrid cattle, crossed between the male buffalo and the domestic cow. They are very tame, taking no more notice of human being than ordinary cattle do. They are very hardy, and seem pre-eminently adapted to ranging our plains. They readily mate and nature seems to provide their offspring with a constitution adapted to all climatic charges of the northwest.—[Drovers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped report of a buffalo–cattle hybrid herd at the Manitoba penitentiary.

articles.text: A few day ago a Mr. Blasing, of Riley county, Kan., missed his cattle, 22 in number, and the next day heard of them being driven towards Manhattan. He found that two strangers, with more enterprise than good judgment had butchered 3 head of them, selling one carcass to local butchers and shipping 2 of them to Kansas City. A telegram with a sheriff at the end of it caught up with the exporters, in Topeka, and they are now, temporarily, gusts of the county. When the returns are all in it will doubtless be found that they are unanimously elected to State positions, with permanent headquarters at Lansing. The minions of the laws seem determined to crush out every attempt to establish what, if undisturbed would develop into a great traffic in dressed meat.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped Kansas cattle-theft story.

articles.text: The following is a distressing picture drawn in a dispatch with reference to the suffering of cattle that were shipped to New York recently, during the hot spells, and clearly demonstrates the advantage of western slaughtered beef against these fever heated animals: "Since Tuesday of last week 20 per cent. of the western cattle have died on the cars or immediately after being transferred to the stock yards. The soap factories are overstocked with carcasses of steers, hogs, and sheep, bought at prices ranging from ten to fifty cents a [head?].—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: A clipped dispatch on western cattle dying after shipment to New York.

articles.text: The first national convention of cattlemen ever held in this country opened its session in St. Louis, Tuesday at the exposition building, which was handsomely fitted up and decorated for the occasion. Delegates were present representing nearly all the western states, territories, several eastern states, Mexico, England and Scotlond. Col. R. S. Hunter, of St. Louis, originator of the project, called the convention to order and announced as the object of the gathering the formation of a national league of cattle intersts for mutual good. Addresses were made by Mayor Ewing, of St. Louis, Gov. Crittenden, Gen. W. T. Sherman and others. A very pleasant and amusing features of the convention is the cow boy band of Fort Dodge, Kan., twenty strong, in full frontier costume. They played several selections during the morning's session, exciting great applause. The leader wields in place of a baton his silver mounted Derringer, nearly a foot long.
articles.summary: Report of the first national cattlemen's convention at St. Louis.

articles.text: One of the most startling and romantic features of border life occurred recently on the Wild Horse praire, thirty miles north of Los Angeles, when a band of wild horses, under the lead of a noble sorrel stallion, came galloping over the plain to reconnoiter a company of surveyors engaged in making a survey of the tract. The band dashed towards Capt. Keller and his party of surveyors till within about 500 feet, when the leader halted in a grandly proud and defiant manner, with neck curved, nostrils distended, erect, and tail on dress parade, and all the band ranged themselves on each side of him like a squad of cavalry in a battle charge. After surveying the scene for a moment the leader galloped proudly away, followed by the band in the most graceful and dignified manner. The scene was most romantic, and the picture of the lordly leader, with his most obedient subjects in their fleet and graceful motions, was worthy of an artist's pencil. There was another band of wild horses on the same prairie, under the leadership of a dark mahogany bay stallion, with black mane, tail and knees. In this band there are two white horses, while the rest are bay and sorrel mainly. Few people are aware that at the base of the Sierra Madre, only thirty miles from this city, wild horses roam in their native beauty and crop the rich grasses that grow on Wild Horse prairie. Yet such is the fact, and their slick appearance and graceful motions are the admiration of all beholders.—[Los Angeles (Cal.) Express.
articles.summary: Clipped Los Angeles Express story of wild horse bands on Wild Horse prairie.

articles.text: A Des Moins, Iowa, corespondent of the St. Paul Pioneer Press writes as follows concerning the mysterious deaths of cattle in Iowa and Minnesota: Two months ago there was great fatality among horses in a western county. The cause was traced to a plant known as wild pea, which grows on bottom lands along rivers all over the state. A recent extended mortality among cattle in the northern part of the state has been traced to another plant, known to botanists as Limnactis minutulia. It is found extensively in Minnesota lakes, in Okoboji and nearly all lakes in Iowa. It appears in July in the shallow water about the shore. It is round, nearly the size of a pinhead, and is suspended in the water in masses. In the latter part of the month it undergoes several changes of color, from a greenish hue to that of frost-bitten grass. It floats in masses on the shore, undergoes decomposition, giving out a peculiar sickening odor, which will be recognizable by every person who has frequented the shores of these lakes in the months of July and August. For several years farmers around Lakes Tetonka and Sakatah, in Minnesota, north of Albert Lea, and around Okoboji, have lost cattle in July in a very sudden and mysterious manner. Apparently well, they would be dead in two hours. So, also, of horses and hogs. The cause was a mystery. It was discovered that the deaths occurred among animals that that had drunk at the lakes, by the fact that of a gang of men at work on a railroad in 1883, one evening several got water from Lake Sakatah; the remainder from a brook. Those that drank at the lake died. This year there was a repetition of the mortality, and it was noticed that this peculiar odor was present around the lake when the animals died. At other seasons animals drank the lake water without injury. A post mortem was made of some of the cattle, and the lining membrane of the stomach showed distinctly the line reached by the water drank. The membrane was sloughing off scalded cuticle. Prof. Stalker, state veterinarian, was called, who has traced the trouble to this plant. He is now investigating the plant to ascertain its poisonous properties.
articles.summary: Clipped report on a lake plant blamed for cattle deaths in Iowa and Minnesota.

articles.text: Last Thursday evening a shooting affray took place between George Heywood and Bob Roberts, Mr. Heywood receiving a painful but not fatal wound. From information gleaned it seems that ill feeling has existed between these two gentlemen for some time, and on the night mentioned they met in a saloon on the other side of the river. Both had been drinking a little, and in the course of the evening some words passed between them, but as far as the shooting is concerned, it is hard to say exactly how it happened. Mr. Heywood had emptied his revolver, and was standing outside the door when a bullet was fired through it and came very near him. He entered the saloon and made some remark, when hot words were indulged in, Mr. Roberts leaving the saloon, telling Heywood not to follow him. Mr. Roberts went to another saloon, and in a short time Heywood put in an appearance, when Roberts fired three shots. Eye-witnesses think the shooting of Heywood was accidental, as Mr. Roberts is an excellent shot and could have killed Heywood had he any intention of doing so. He sent two balls through the ceiling, and it is thought the third was intended to be high, but the revolver went off half-cocked, the ball striking Heywood in the left breast, tearing the flesh and passing through his left arm. Roberts and Heywood are good citizens, and it is to be hoped that nothing serious will be the result of this little misunderstanding.
articles.summary: George Heywood was wounded when Bob Roberts fired three shots in a Medora saloon after a quarrel; witnesses thought the hit accidental.

articles.summary: The roller rink announces Tuesday and Friday hours and new skates.

articles.headline: Our New Confectionery.
articles.text: Mr. Charles Cook wishes to announce to the people of Medora and vicinity that he has on hand a full stock of confectionery, nuts, fruits, and everything usually kept in a store of this kind. He carries a full stock of tobacco, smoking and chewing, pipes and smokers' articles. Mr. Cook also has a fine line of stationery, and any one wishing anything in his line of business should call and examine his stock.
articles.summary: Charles Cook announces his new confectionery in Medora.

articles.text:
City Drug Store, Medora, Dak., H. M. Jorgens, Proprietor — drugs, patent medicines, perfumery, toilet articles, notions, periodicals, stationery; "Pure liquors for medical purposes always on hand."
Mayville Stock Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak. — Short Horn bulls for sale; J. L. & E. B. Grandin, Props.; W. W. Warren, General Manager.
Hardware and Tinware at J. D. Garver's, Little Missouri, Dak. — tin and sheet-iron articles made and repaired.
Northern Pacific Railroad — "Going East or Going West, no matter which, the Northern Pacific Railroad is your line"; St. Paul to Portland, Ore., Yellowstone National Park; Chas. S. Fee, General Passenger Agent, St. Paul.
General Store of the N. P. R. C. Co., Medora, Dakota — groceries, dry goods, ready-made clothing, hats, caps, canned goods, harness, saddles, tobacco and cigars, felt shoes, overshoes, boots and shoes, flour and feed; "Hunters Outfits a Specialty"; wholesale and retail.
Medora Stage & F. Co., A. T. Packard, General Manager, Medora — horse brand on left shoulder; horses strung on stage stations between Medora and Deadwood; $25 reward for arrest of anyone dealing unlawfully with these horses.
Supply Depot for Milwaukee Beer by the case, keg or car load — C. B. Williams & Co., Bismarck, Dak.
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, fancy bits and spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores.
Minneapolis & St. Louis Ry, "The Famous Albert Lea Route" — through trains Minneapolis and St. Paul to Chicago and St. Louis; S. F. Boyd, Gen'l Tkt. & Pass. Agt., Minneapolis.
Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars, case & bar goods.
articles.summary: Display advertisements in columns 2–4 of page 4.

articles.text:
Brand: E. W. Casey & Co., Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co., Dak. — KC and F, 1st brand on left hip and shoulder, 2nd without circle; range O'Donnell creek.
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P.O. Medora — brand on left hip; range Little Missouri 7 miles south of N. P. R. R.; horse brand on left shoulder.
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, M'g'r, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — VI on left hip, horse brand same; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river.
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — V V V on left side, also one or two V's on either side; ear mark under-bit in left ear; range Belle Fourche.
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 on left side; ear mark left ear cropped; range Grand river; additional brands ZD, DZ, ZD (bar), circle cross; $100 reward re VVV or E6 ranges.
Brand: H. R. Tarbell & Co., Medora, Dak. — H on left shoulder (horse); range Davis creek and Little Missouri river.
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — TD on left hip; ear mark tip of left ear cut off square; vent bar under T. D.; additional brands quarter-circle diamond on left side and T on left hip.
Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora — LC on left side and reversed C on right hip; range Little Missouri south of the R. R.; ranch Tepee bottom; ear mark crop the right; horse brand LC on left shoulder; owners of DW brand.
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — SO on left side; ear marks swallow fork right ear and crop left; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek, north of N. P. R. R.
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora, Dak. — JP (and a second brand) and Y-cross brand on left side, horse brand same; also owner of steers bought of Mason & Lovell branded -H- and 7Z; calf mark left ear grubbed; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — R in circle on left hip and side or left hip only; ear marks both ears swallow forked; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river.
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777 on right hip, side and shoulder; ear mark grub the right ear; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora, Dak. — six-inch circle-dot on both sides (cattle), four-inch circle-dot on left shoulder and left hip (horses); range six miles north of crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri.
Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — RR and JP horse brands for horses and mules; ranch four miles down river from crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri.
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora — LSF on left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek.
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., [A.?] Alden Eaton, Supt., P.O. Medora — HK in circle[?] on left side, swallow fork right ear; 2nd brand on right side; 3rd brand on left hip; horse brand on left hip; range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis creeks.
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX on right side, additional V on both sides; ear marks left ear cropped and under hacked, right cropped; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Manager, P.O. Medora — 7L on right hip and shoulder, bellows on left hip or shoulder, Pd on left hip and shoulder; range Little Missouri river fifteen miles north of Medora.
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P.O. Medora — thistle on left or right shoulder; range Keogh crossing of Little Missouri to Pretty butte; vent bar under thistle; 2nd brand (triangle JP[?]) on left or right shoulder; 3rd brand anywhere on animal, young stock.
articles.summary: Cattle- and horse-brand advertisements filling columns 5–7 of page 4.

events.title: Capitol building at Bismarck turned over to Dakota Territory
events.summary: The capital commission turned the new capitol at Bismarck over to the territory and notified the governor, as the capital commission act required.
events.excerpt: The capitol building at Bismarck was turned over to the territory by the capital commission

events.title: J. L. White returns from two-week hunt with sixteen deer
events.summary: J. L. White came back from a two weeks' hunting expedition with sixteen deer; Vic Smith went along.
events.excerpt: He succeeded in killing sixteen deer, and is much pleased with the result.

events.title: Platt Bristol and David Howe of Mandan visit Medora on business
events.summary: Platt Bristol and David Howe of Mandan came in on Saturday's train on business and predicted a brilliant future for Medora.
events.excerpt: Both of these gentlemen are highly pleased with Medora, and predict a brilliant future for us.

events.title: Vocalist John Kelly to perform at the Hotel de Mores
events.summary: California vocalist John Kelly, passing through with his wife, agreed to give an entertainment in the Hotel de Mores dining-room, offered by Mr. Fitzgerald; admission 50 cents.
events.excerpt: give an entertainment to-morrow night in the dining-room of Hotel de Mores, kindly tendered him by Mr. Fitzgerald.

events.date_basis: "recently"; no date given, week before issue
events.title: George Grinnell reported hanged by Montana stranglers
events.summary: George Grinnell, well known in the region, was reported hanged by the Montana stranglers; locally he was said not to be a cattle thief, and the hanging was blamed on an old quarrel over buffalo robes.
events.excerpt: was reported to have been hanged by the Montana Stranglers recently.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday's east bound train" before Thu 20 Nov 1884
events.title: False buffalo alarm sends de Morès and Van Driesche riding out; Eaton's tame buffalo spared
events.summary: A train passenger reported buffalo four miles from town and telegraphed hunters from Belfield; riders including the Marquis de Morès and William Van Driesche set out, but the animals were Howard Eaton's tame buffalo.
events.excerpt: it was hard to tell whether the Marquis de Mores or William VanDriesche would get the first shot.

events.date_basis: "Thanksgiving Eve, Wednesday, November 26th" stated; issue Thu 20 Nov 1884
events.title: Thanksgiving Eve grand ball at Robert's hall
events.summary: A social dance was announced for Thanksgiving Eve in Robert's hall under the management of James Hannigan, open to the public.
events.excerpt: On Thanksgiving Eve, Wednesday, November 26th, a social dance will be given in Robert's hall under the management of Mr. James Hannigan.

events.date_basis: standing notice; no date given, week before issue
events.title: Cattlemen offer $250 reward against grass-fire setters
events.summary: The N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Continental Cattle Co., Hughes & Simpson, Dorr Clark, Clark & Plum, Dickey Bros. and E. G. Paddock offered $250 for the arrest of anyone setting fire to the grass in western Dakota's cattle sections.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass

events.date_basis: notice; no date given, week before issue
events.title: Gregor Lang offers $50 for missing horses
events.summary: Gregor Lang offered $50 for the return of a bay, a brown and a roan mare and a sorrel pony carrying his advertised brands.
events.excerpt: One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young

events.date_basis: notice; no date given, week before issue
events.title: Horse lost from the Little Missouri round-up
events.summary: W. N. Thompson & Co. offered $10 for a five-year-old bay horse branded J and S, lost from the Little Missouri round-up with a picket rope around its neck.
events.excerpt: Lost from the Little Missouri round-up, one bay horse 5 years old

events.title: Sorrel horse strays from the Medora stage company
events.summary: A sorrel horse with four white feet strayed from the M. S. & F. Co.; the company offered $25 for information.
events.excerpt: From M. S. & F. Co., October 5, one sorrel horse

events.date_basis: standing report; no date given, week before issue
events.title: Glendive paper calls Crow reservation a haven for horse thieves
events.summary: Quoting the Glendive Times, the paper reported 300 to 400 stolen horses cached near Black canyon on the Crow reservation.
events.excerpt: There are said to be from 300 to 400 head of stolen herses cached in the vicinity of Black canyon

events.date_basis: no date given, week before issue
events.title: Medora slaughter house nears completion
events.summary: The slaughter house was reported fast nearing completion.
events.excerpt: The slaughter house is fast nearing completion.

events.date_basis: advertisement; no date given, week before issue
events.title: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. offers its whole cattle herd for sale
events.summary: Wishing to confine itself to beef cattle, the N. P. Ref. Car Co. advertised its herd of about 700 she cattle and 250 steers, plus 65 bulls and 55 she cattle, on Beaver creek, Dawson county, Montana.
events.excerpt: We offer for sale our entire herd of AMERICAN CATTLE

events.title: Bob Roberts goes to Bismarck
events.summary: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck.
events.excerpt: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck Monday.

events.title: Vic Smith leaves with a Russian nobleman for an extended hunt
events.summary: Hunter Vic Smith was to leave with a Russian nobleman for an extended hunt.
events.excerpt: Vic Smith will leave to-day with a Russian nobleman for an extended hunt.

events.date_basis: no date given, week before issue
events.title: Stage company buys ten carloads of grain for its line
events.summary: The M. S. & F. Co. bought ten carloads of grain to distribute along its line.
events.excerpt: The M. S. & F. Co. purchased ten car loads of grain, which will be distributed along its line.

events.date_basis: no date given, week before issue
events.title: Peter Book closes his brick business for the season
events.summary: Peter Book had about closed his business for the season and was well satisfied with the results.
events.excerpt: Peter Book has about closed his business for the season.

events.date_basis: no date given, week before issue
events.title: Ellison's ice dam across the Little Missouri nearly finished
events.summary: Mr. Ellison had nearly completed a dam across the Little Missouri and expected a big ice harvest.
events.excerpt: Mr. Ellison has nearly completed the dam across the Little Missouri, and expects to reap a big ice harvest.

events.title: Packard leaves for Governor Pierce's reception in Bismarck
events.summary: Editor A. T. Packard left for Bismarck to attend Governor Pierce's reception and was expected home Saturday.
events.excerpt: A. T. Packard left for Bismarck Monday to attend Governor Pierce's reception.

events.title: Carload of N. P. R. C. Co. beef wrecked near Dickinson
events.summary: A carload of beef shipped by the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. was wrecked near Dickinson and the meat badly damaged.
events.excerpt: A car load of beef shipped by the N. P. R. C. Co. was wrecked near Dickinson Wednesday.

events.title: Mandan dentist Dr. E. E. Ball arrives in Medora
events.summary: Dr. E. E. Ball of Mandan arrived and set up at John O'Sullivan's barber shop to do dental work.
events.excerpt: Dr. E. E. Ball, of Mandan, arrived in town last evening, and is located at Mr. John O' Sullivan's barber shop.

events.title: John Monroe builds cut-off on the Medora–Deadwood stage line
events.summary: John Monroe completed a cut-off on the M. S. & F. Co.'s line, shortening it about a mile and avoiding the only hill on the route.
events.excerpt: This shortens the distance about a mile and avoids the only hill on the route.

events.title: Furniture arrives for William Van Driesche's house
events.summary: Furniture for William Van Driesche's house arrived; he said he would move in once his wife came from Europe.
events.excerpt: will be occupied by him as soon as his wife comes from Europe.

events.title: Deadwood stage brings passengers in record 36 hours
events.summary: Tuesday's stage from Deadwood made the trip in 36 hours and 5 minutes, bringing Mr. and Mrs. N. C. Ludgen, H. M. Janlund, E. D. Morse, M. Franke, O. Kinley and W. Tolbert.
events.excerpt: Tuesday's stage from Deadwood made the trip in 36 hours and 5 minutes.

events.title: Montana stock inspector Thomas Matthews in Medora
events.summary: Thomas Matthews, cattle inspector for the Montana Stock Growers' Association, was in town and said cattle shipments were about over for the season.
events.excerpt: He reports cattle shipments about over for the season.

events.date_basis: no date given, week before issue
events.title: Pat O'Hara stops Sunday coal deliveries
events.summary: Pat O'Hara announced he would no longer deliver coal on Sunday; orders could be left at the Cow Boy office.
events.excerpt: no more coal will be delivered on Sunday.

events.title: Fisher's new houses finished; Cook and Garver move in
events.summary: J. C. Fisher's houses were completed; one was occupied by confectioner Charles Cook and the other was to be taken by tinsmith Mr. Garver the first of next week.
events.excerpt: Mr. Fisher's houses are completed.

events.title: Northern Pacific train times to change at Medora
events.summary: It was reported that train times would change on the 23d: the morning train half an hour later, the evening train an hour earlier.
events.excerpt: It is reported that the time of the trains will be changed on the 23d inst.

events.title: Bob Roberts wounds George Heywood in saloon shooting
events.summary: After ill feeling and words in a saloon across the river, Bob Roberts fired three shots in another saloon; one struck George Heywood in the left breast and passed through his arm. Witnesses thought the hit accidental.
events.excerpt: Last Thursday evening a shooting affray took place between George Heywood and Bob Roberts, Mr. Heywood receiving a painful but not fatal wound.

events.title: J. A. Ferris opens a feed stable in Little Missouri
events.summary: J. A. Ferris of Little Missouri arranged to shelter and feed horses of ranchmen and others while in town.
events.excerpt: has completed arrangements whereby he can accommodate ranchmen and all others who wish to shelter and feed their horses

events.title: Roller rink sets Tuesday and Friday hours
events.summary: The roller skating rink announced it would open Tuesday and Friday afternoons and evenings, with new skates arrived.
events.excerpt: the roller skating rink will be open on Tuesday and Friday afternoons and evenings.

events.title: Charles Cook opens a confectionery in Medora
events.summary: Charles Cook announced a full stock of confectionery, nuts, fruits, tobacco and stationery.
events.excerpt: Mr. Charles Cook wishes to announce to the people of Medora and vicinity that he has on hand a full stock of confectionery
